title: CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393) SR&ED Ruling
subject: FCA appeal on whether lottery ticket marketing software qualified as SR&ED under Regulation 2900.
summary: C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, is a Federal Court of Appeal decision affirming the Tax Court's denial of SR&ED claims for in-house custom lottery software in the 1991 to 1995 taxation years. For Canadian taxpayers claiming SR&ED, its key takeaway is the five-criterion test: technological uncertainty, targeted hypotheses, scientific method, technological advancement and contemporaneous documentation.
metaDescription: Read the 2001 FCA 393 SR&ED ruling for CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada and learn how the Federal Court of Appeal assesses Canadian R&D claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Overview of the Dispute

The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (also cited as C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2002 DTC 6740, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 212, [2001] F.C.J. No. 1886 (QL)), affirming the judgment of the Tax Court of Canada in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 2372, [2000] 4 C.T.C. 2272 (Court File No. 98-1324(IT)G), stands as one of the foundational appellate authorities governing Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives in Canada. Heard on appeal from the decision of Judge M.J. Bonner of the Tax Court of Canada rendered on August 30, 2000, the litigation addressed whether the in-house development of custom application software constituted "scientific research and experimental development" (SRED) within the meaning of section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, such that the current and capital expenditures claimed for the 1991 to 1995 taxation years qualified for the SR&ED incentives under the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act").

In the underlying dispute, the appellant taxpayer, C.W. Agencies Inc.—which carried on the business of marketing tickets in government-sponsored lotteries to customers in many parts of the world by telephone and computer in a number of languages, had two to three million customers, and received as many as 25,000 purchase orders in a day—developed in-house a customized computer application software system known as the International Distributed Lottery System ("IDLS"), because no ready-made software could meet its requirements of flexibility, scalability, instant response time, accuracy and reliability; in doing so, it used an IBM AS/400 platform based on then-emerging object-oriented technology, the Synon CASE (computer-aided software engineering) tool, and a rapid prototype methodology rather than the then-traditional "waterfall" methodology. The taxpayer claimed the cost of the developers and consultants directly involved in this development process, arguing that the development of the IDLS constituted scientific research as defined in Regulation 2900 for the purposes of section 37 of the Act. Upon audit and technical review, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the tax administration (then Revenue Canada, now the Canada Revenue Agency or "CRA"), assessed the taxpayer for the 1991 to 1995 taxation years so as to disallow the claimed SRED current and capital expenditures; the expenditure figures themselves were agreed by the parties, and the case was fought on an all-or-nothing basis.

The Minister's challenge rested on the determination that the taxpayer's custom software development activities did not constitute a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" undertaken for the purposes of achieving "technological advancement" within the meaning of subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations (the predecessor of the current definition in subsection 248(1) of the Act). Rather, the Crown's evidence—from Robert Thomas Arnold, the consultant to Revenue Canada who reviewed the claim, and from its expert witness, Dr. Ken Takagaki—was that the overall activities were routine in nature, involved no technological uncertainty that could not be resolved by standard practices or routine engineering, and amounted to routine information systems development by competent and prudent users of commercially available technologies, using the information systems development methodologies and practices current at the time. Furthermore, Dr. Takagaki observed that the general hypothesis advanced for the projects—that each project was not achievable in a cost-effective manner given the state of the art of computing technology—turned on many economic variables beyond technical or scientific factors; separately, the hypothesis described by the taxpayer's own expert, Dr. Jacob Slonim—that the object-oriented architecture would yield higher productivity per person from the reusability of components and a decrease in system development time compared to procedurally based development methods—was found by Judge Bonner to be too vague to be proved or disproved by scientific research and, in any event, not shown to have been tested.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

During the taxation years at issue (1991 to 1995), the definition governing SR&ED claims was found in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations"), for the purposes of sections 37 and 37.1 of the Income Tax Act (one version applied to the 1991 and 1992 taxation years and an amended version to taxation years ending after December 2, 1992); throughout subsequent Canadian jurisprudence, the legal architecture governing SR&ED claims has been anchored in interlocking provisions of the Act and the Regulations, supplemented by administrative guidelines issued by the tax authority. Following the migration of the substantive definition from section 2900 of the Regulations into subsection 248(1) of the Act, "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The definition divides eligible core work into three distinct categories: paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph 248(1)(b) covers applied research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and paragraph 248(1)(c) governs experimental development, namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Under paragraph 248(1)(d), where a taxpayer establishes qualifying work under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer, eligible SR&ED also encompasses directly supporting work—specifically engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—provided such work is "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" the core experimental development or scientific research. Crucially, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude commercial and routine activities from SR&ED eligibility, barring claims for work with respect to market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e), quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes under paragraph (f), research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g), mineral, petroleum, or natural gas prospecting, exploring, drilling, or producing under paragraph (h), the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i), style changes under paragraph (j), and routine data collection under paragraph (k).

In tandem with subsection 248(1), sections 37 and 127 of the Act establish the expenditure deduction and tax credit mechanics. Section 37 permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by or on behalf of the taxpayer, allowing unclaimed expenditures to be carried forward in the taxpayer's SR&ED expenditure pool. Subsection 127(5) and the definitions in subsection 127(9) provide for Investment Tax Credits calculated as a statutory percentage of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" pool, which subsection 127(18) reduces by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments received or receivable by the taxpayer. To access these incentives, taxpayers must file prescribed technical and financial information on Form T661 within the statutory filing deadline. While not legally binding on the Courts, Information Circular 86-4R3 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development) and the sector-specific Information Circular 97-1 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development — Administrative Guidelines for Software Development, dated February 28, 1997) articulated the administrative framework used by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) to evaluate technological uncertainty, technological advancement, and systematic investigation; the CRA's current administrative guidance is set out in its Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, dated August 13, 2021. In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), Judge Bowman recognized that IC 86-4R3 provides a reliable, practical exposition of the technical thresholds intended by Parliament, and the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 subsequently embedded those conceptual pillars into binding appellate case law.
The Court's Final Holding and Doctrinal Significance

Both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal ruled against the taxpayer, dismissing the appeal and upholding the Minister's reassessments. At the Tax Court level, Judge Bonner subjected the taxpayer's custom software project to the five-step analytical framework earlier articulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic. Judge Bonner preferred the evidence of the Crown's expert, Dr. Takagaki, over that of the taxpayer's expert, Dr. Slonim, whose conclusions rested on conjecture as to what must have happened, and found that the IDLS, although large and complex, was not shown to be anything more than routine information systems development or more than a variation on products already in existence. Specifically, commenting on the hypothesis described by Dr. Slonim—that the object-oriented architecture would yield increased productivity per person and reduced system development time—Judge Bonner observed at paragraph 23 that it was not clear that it was capable of being proved or disproved by scientific research because it was simply too vague, noting that a hypothesis in this context is normally considered to mean "a provisional concept which is not inconsistent with known facts and serves as a starting point for further investigation by which it may be proved or disproved objectively". He added that, even if the hypothesis could be tested by scientific research, it did not appear that the taxpayer attempted to test it, since all the taxpayer really attempted to do was to develop software, and he dismissed the appeal with costs.

Upon further appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 unanimously affirmed Judge Bonner's dismissal. In reasons delivered from the Bench at Toronto on December 11, 2001 by Sexton J.A. (Stone and Evans JJ.A. concurring), the Court held that it was the prerogative of the Tax Court Judge to prefer the Crown's expert, noted that the taxpayer had not retained documentation that might have helped it discharge its onus and had called no witness directly and personally involved in the development, and, at paragraph 17, observing that both sides relied on the test in Northwest Hydraulic, set out the five criteria that Judge Bowman had outlined there as useful in determining whether a particular activity constitutes SRED, criteria previously approved by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie. First, the Court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the Court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the inquiry evaluates whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the Court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, the Court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

The doctrinal impact of C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 on Canadian tax law is profound. While Northwest Hydraulic (1998) introduced the five questions at the trial level and RIS-Christie (1998) approved that general approach, C.W. Agencies (2001) reaffirmed at the appellate level the same five-point formulation, which Tax Court judges and Federal Court of Appeal panels have applied for over two decades across all industrial sectors, from custom software and enterprise IT to metallurgy, plastics thermoforming, food science, and automated manufacturing. When taxpayers in subsequent appellate litigation—such as Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88—attempted to argue that the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion improperly imported a "scientific method" requirement not explicitly written in the text of subsection 248(1) of the Act, the Federal Court of Appeal flatly rejected the challenge, holding that Judge Bowman had set out the criteria in interpreting the statutory definition, that courts interpret such provisions through a textual, contextual and purposive analysis, and that the Court had repeatedly endorsed that approach, including in C.W. Agencies.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous forensic analysis of C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393—viewed alongside the underlying Tax Court findings (2000 DTC 2372) and the body of Canadian jurisprudence applying paragraph 17 of the FCA ruling—reveals five interrelated legal, technical, and evidentiary failures that caused the complete disqualification of the taxpayer's claim.
Failure 1: Absence of Genuine Technological Uncertainty Versus Routine Software Engineering and Architectural Selection

The threshold barrier in C.W. Agencies—captured in Criterion 1 of paragraph 17 of the FCA decision—requires the taxpayer to prove the existence of "a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures". As established in Northwest Hydraulic and reiterated through C.W. Agencies, "routine engineering" encompasses techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field of science or technology. Technological uncertainty exists only when whether a given technical result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience in the public domain. Crucially, the uncertainty must stem from an identifiable shortcoming, constraint, or limitation in the underlying state of technology itself, rather than a gap in the internal experience or familiarity of the taxpayer's personnel.

In C.W. Agencies, the taxpayer's project centered on developing the IDLS, a customized lottery ticket order-entry and fulfillment system, in-house using an object-oriented technology platform, a CASE tool and rapid prototyping, in place of the then-standard procedural languages and waterfall development model. The taxpayer conflated the commercial and technical complexity of adopting a modern software architecture with genuine technological uncertainty. While building a large and complex information system with these tools required substantial system design, prototyping, testing and refinement, the Crown's expert, whose evidence was preferred, characterized those activities as routine information systems development using commercially available products and the systems development methodologies and practices widely described in textbooks and taught in post-secondary curricula at the time.

Canadian courts applying C.W. Agencies have consistently enforced a strict legal demarcation between project or technical uncertainty and technological uncertainty. In Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, the Tax Court applied C.W. Agencies to disallow a custom software claim evaluated alongside IC 97-1, holding that resolving functional uncertainties associated with building a complex software product does not equate to resolving technological uncertainties where the existing technological knowledge base is sufficient to solve the problem. Similarly, in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65 (2015 DTC 1089), the Court applied C.W. Agencies to reject an SR&ED claim for a web-crawler software program capable of inspecting and verifying websites, concluding that the work constituted normal analyses and development carried out by competent programmers using current technology and standard software development techniques. Likewise, in Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32, where a taxpayer tested thousands of combinations of existing machine and software settings without modifying the underlying equipment or exceeding its normal operating envelope, the Court held under C.W. Agencies that operating within the designed parameters of commercial technology involves no technological uncertainty. C.W. Agencies failed at this first hurdle because, as the Federal Court of Appeal noted at paragraph 18, the Crown's expert testified that there was no uncertainty that could not be resolved by the application of standard practices or routine engineering, and it was open to the Tax Court Judge to rely on that evidence; Judge Bonner regarded the many "uncertainties" listed by the taxpayer's expert as challenges, and held that whether the software would be suitable for the taxpayer's business was not in itself a matter of technological uncertainty.
Failure 2: Defective Hypothesis Formulation—Non-Falsifiability, Absence of Quantifiable Technical Variables, and Business/Productivity Objectives

The most distinctive jurisprudential contribution of the C.W. Agencies litigation lies in its rigorous dissection of Criterion 2: "Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?". Under the five-stage sub-process integrated into the C.W. Agencies standard, formulating and testing a hypothesis requires the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

In C.W. Agencies, the taxpayer's expert witness, Dr. Jacob Slonim, described the taxpayer's hypothesis as being "that the benefit gained from the object-oriented architecture would result in a higher productivity per person from the reusability of components and a decrease in system development time compared to procedurally based development methods". Judge Bonner at the Tax Court (at paragraph 23) questioned whether this purported hypothesis was capable of being proved or disproved by scientific research, finding it simply too vague and, in any event, not shown to have been tested; the Federal Court of Appeal in 2001 FCA 393 did not separately address the hypothesis but dismissed the appeal from his judgment. The three grounds discussed below combine Judge Bonner's observations with broader analytical commentary.

First, Judge Bonner noted the meaning normally given to the word "hypothesis" in this context, namely "a provisional concept which is not inconsistent with known facts and serves as a starting point for further investigation by which it may be proved or disproved objectively". To be proved or disproved objectively, a hypothesis must be verifiable by means of observation and empirical measurement. Judge Bonner found that it was not clear that C.W. Agencies' hypothesis was capable of being proved or disproved by scientific research, as it was simply too vague, and that, even if it could be tested, the taxpayer did not appear to have attempted to test it. Although neither court made this observation, it may be noted analytically that, in a commercial business context, a company does not typically write the exact same custom software application twice—once using an object-oriented architecture and a second time using a procedurally based development method under controlled baseline conditions—merely to measure and compare programmer productivity per person and elapsed system development time. Without a controlled baseline or a comparative experimental protocol capable of isolating architectural effects on development time, the statement was an unverifiable assertion rather than an objectively testable scientific hypothesis.

Second, as an analytical matter (this ground was not part of Judge Bonner's reasons, and both courts rejected the notion that activity undertaken with a business purpose in view is for that reason alone excluded from SRED), the hypothesis described by the taxpayer's expert targeted an economic, managerial, and labour-productivity metric ("higher productivity per person" and "decrease in system development time") rather than a scientific or technological uncertainty. Under subsection 248(1) and Criterion 2 of C.W. Agencies, the hypothesis must be "specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty". A valid SR&ED hypothesis must articulate a causal relationship between an independent technical variable (such as an algorithmic data structure, memory allocation protocol, or concurrency lock mechanism) and a proposed quantifiable technological effect (such as deterministic sub-millisecond latency under thread contention or memory overhead scaling). By framing its hypothesis around human developer efficiency and project delivery schedules, C.W. Agencies described a business management objective rather than a technological proposition.

Third, a valid hypothesis must propose a causal relationship that goes beyond known or expected effects of existing technology. Component reusability and modular maintainability are the foundational, textbook characteristics of object-oriented programming. Proposing that adopting an object-oriented architecture will yield component reuse is merely restating the known design purpose of the paradigm. As subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence applying C.W. Agencies confirmed—such as Advanced Agricultural Testing Inc. v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 190—where a taxpayer merely applies existing products or architectures to observe their expected performance without varying technical parameters to test an unknown causal mechanism, no scientific hypothesis has been formulated.
Failure 3: Absence of the Total Discipline of the Scientific Method and Reliance on Ad Hoc Development

Criterion 3 of C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (para. 17) asks: "Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?". In the original Northwest Hydraulic formulation endorsed by the FCA, this criterion requires that the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by "trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses".

In C.W. Agencies, Judge Bonner found that, even if the hypothesis described by the taxpayer's expert could be tested, the taxpayer did not appear to have attempted to test it, and that all the taxpayer really attempted to do was to develop software. Although the taxpayer proceeded in a systematic fashion (as the reviewing consultant admitted) and used the AS/400 performance utility to compare prototype configurations, the Crown's expert characterized its work as identifying requirements, creating prototypes with the CASE tool, testing, design refinement and iteration—routine systems development using commonly applied methodologies—directed at defining business requirements, evaluating commercial products, testing hardware configurations and routine software testing, rather than at systematically formulating, testing and modifying hypotheses to resolve a technological uncertainty.

Canadian courts applying Criterion 3 of C.W. Agencies have repeatedly emphasized that "trial and error" coding or empirical tinkering does not satisfy the statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis" under subsection 248(1). In Maritime-Ontario Freight Lines Limited v. The Queen, 2003 TCC 674, and Flavor Net Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 179, the Tax Court relied on the C.W. Agencies framework to distinguish systematic experimentation from blind trial and error, holding that trial and error occurs when tests are conducted without a clear theoretical hypothesis guiding the selection of variables and without a logical chain of analysis linking one test to the next. Similarly, in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (aff'd 2022 FCA 72)—a software development appeal where the Court actually accepted that the taxpayer faced genuine technological uncertainty under Criterion 1 regarding multi-tenant architecture record-set paging, in-memory pivot array initialization, and deterministic stateful client-side controls—Justice Lafleur nevertheless dismissed the appeal under Criteria 2 and 3 of C.W. Agencies. The Court held that the software developer could not demonstrate a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests," proving that even when genuine technological uncertainty exists, ad hoc software coding without methodical hypothesis testing and modification is fatal to an SR&ED claim. Furthermore, as the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (citing C.W. Agencies, 2001 FCA 393 at para. 17), taxpayers cannot evade Criterion 3 by arguing that the phrase "scientific method" is absent from subsection 248(1) of the Act; the scientific method is the mandatory legal standard by which Canadian courts interpret "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis".
Failure 4: Conflation of Functional Product Creation with Technological Advancement

Under Criterion 4 of C.W. Agencies (para. 17), the Court asks: "Did the process result in a technological advancement?". For experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) of the Act, the work must be undertaken "for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto".

A pervasive legal failure exhibited in C.W. Agencies and subsequent software and engineering disputes is the taxpayer's assumption that because a project resulted in a new, customized, or commercially superior software system or physical product, it necessarily achieved a "technological advancement". Under the C.W. Agencies doctrine, the creation of a new product or custom software application—even one that is novel in the taxpayer's industry or market—does not in itself constitute a technological advancement. Rather, the process must generate new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the understanding of scientific relations or technologies—that is, it must advance the taxpayer's and the industry's technological knowledge base beyond what was publicly available or deducible by a competent professional.

Importantly, the Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies framework recognizes that a project does not need to succeed commercially or even achieve its initial technical objective to satisfy Criterion 4: the rejection after systematic testing of a formal hypothesis is nonetheless a technological advance because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis and reinforces the measure of the technological uncertainty. Similarly, the technological advancement sought or achieved only has to be slight or incremental to qualify under paragraph 248(1)(c). However, in C.W. Agencies, the Crown's expert testified that, because there was no uncertainty that could not be resolved by standard practices or routine engineering, the software could not constitute a technological advancement (2001 FCA 393, para. 18); Judge Bonner found that the IDLS, although heavily customized, large and complex, was not shown to be anything more than a variation on products already in existence, and that resolving the taxpayer expert's "uncertainties" by avoidance or by "ugly or temporary solutions" did not necessarily constitute technological advancement.
Failure 5: Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation, Post-Hoc Reconstructions, and Costing/Contractual Vulnerabilities

The fifth criterion set out in paragraph 17 of C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 asks: "Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?". This evidentiary requirement derives from Judge Bowman's observation in Northwest Hydraulic (approved in RIS-Christie and C.W. Agencies) that although the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations do not state so explicitly, "it seems self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results be kept, and that it be kept as the work progresses".

In Canadian tax litigation, the legal status of contemporaneous documentation under Criterion 5 of C.W. Agencies involves a critical nuance that practitioners must navigate with precision. As Justice Archambault noted in 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] A.C.I. No. 478 (QL), and as Justice Jorré emphasized in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, and Justice Lafleur noted in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47, the Income Tax Act does not make the existence of contemporaneous written test reports a strict statutory condition precedent for SR&ED recognition; in principle, a taxpayer may adduce evidence of systematic investigation through credible oral testimony. However, as the Courts warn, any taxpayer attempting to convince the Minister or the Tax Court that it performed a systematic scientific investigation without progressive, contemporaneous records places itself in a "very precarious position" where the entire claim hinges on judicial assessments of witness credibility and memory years after the fact.

In C.W. Agencies, the taxpayer did not retain documentation (including a detailed project management plan) that might have assisted it in discharging its onus, and called no witness directly and personally involved in the development; its expert was compelled to examine the results of the work and the electronic logs generated by the CASE tool and to infer the problems faced and the steps taken, conclusions Judge Bonner found to rest on conjecture (2001 FCA 393, paras. 10–11). In its progeny, taxpayers routinely fail Criterion 5 when their documentary record consists solely of commercial design specifications, source code repositories without experimental logs, or retrospective narratives drafted by external SR&ED consultants after the taxation year has closed. For example, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd., 2019 TCC 246 (aff'd 2021 FCA 88), Justice Owen found that the complete absence of progressive experimental documentation—save for after-the-fact summaries prepared by the appellant's SR&ED consultant—was fatal to proving a systematic investigation. Similarly, in Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC), applying C.W. Agencies, the Tax Court dismissed the claim because the taxpayer's test description documents lacked specific hypotheses, observations, conclusions, or test purposes, and the test summaries lacked timesheets or records identifying the specific prototypes subjected to each test.

Even where technical documentation exists, claims fail when taxpayers cannot substantiate the nexus between qualified SR&ED activities (including directly supporting work under paragraph 248(1)(d)) and the financial expenditures claimed under sections 37 and 127. In Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32, applying C.W. Agencies, the company president estimated at year-end that 10.2% of employees' time pertained to SR&ED activities and claimed 10.2% of total salaries. The Tax Court flatly rejected this method, holding that arbitrary or retrospective percentage estimates of hours worked are legally insufficient to justify SR&ED expenditure claims under the Act. Furthermore, where testing occurs on commercial production lines or within custom client deliverables without strict governance protocols segregating "experimental development deviations" from commercial production (excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i)) or routine quality control testing (excluded under paragraph 248(1)(f)), or without clear contractual terms establishing that the SR&ED was performed "by or on behalf of the taxpayer" uncommitted to a third-party "contract payment" reduction under subsection 127(9), the claim is vulnerable to complete disallowance.
3. Comparative Summary Table
Mapping the C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393) Legal Requirements Against Taxpayer Failures and Judicial Standards of Proof

The following table maps each of the five criteria (originating in Northwest Hydraulic and approved in RIS-Christie) set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17), alongside the supplementary statutory requirements of subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the Income Tax Act, against the specific failures exhibited by the taxpayer and the governing standard of proof enforced by Canadian courts.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in C.W. Agencies & Progeny
Judicial Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Threshold

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Existence of a scientific or technological obstacle not removable by routine engineering or standard procedures)
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, para. 17 (Criterion 1); Northwest Hydraulic, 98 DTC 1839, para. 16; Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(a)–(c).

Relied on the size and complexity of developing the IDLS with an object-oriented platform, a CASE tool and rapid prototyping as evidence of technological uncertainty. The Crown's preferred expert testified that there was no uncertainty that could not be resolved by standard practices or routine engineering, and that the work used commercially available products and current information systems development methodologies and practices.

The taxpayer must establish on a balance of probabilities (Hickman Motors prima facie standard) that whether a technical objective could be achieved, or how to achieve it, was not known or determinable based on generally available scientific or technological knowledge and experience in the public domain. Must identify the exact shortcoming or limitation in the underlying state of technology, distinct from internal skill gaps or routine engineering.
2. Formulation of Targeted, Verifiable Hypotheses (Provisional concepts specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty)
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, para. 17 (Criterion 2); C.W. Agencies (TCC), 2000 DTC 2372, para. 23; Advanced Agricultural Testing, 2009 TCC 190.

Its expert described a hypothesis that object-oriented architecture would yield higher per-person productivity from component reuse and decrease system development time compared to procedurally based methods; Judge Bonner found it simply too vague to be proved or disproved by scientific research and, in any event, not shown to have been tested, since all the taxpayer really attempted to do was to develop software.

The taxpayer must prove the formulation of a "provisional concept which is not inconsistent with known facts and serves as a starting point for further investigation by which it may be proved or disproved objectively" (Bonner J., para. 23). The hypothesis must link an independent technological variable to a proposed quantifiable effect beyond known or expected effects, and must be empirically verifiable by observation.
3. Total Discipline of the Scientific Method (Systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis, including testing and modification of hypotheses)

C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, para. 17 (Criterion 3); Kam-Press Metal Products, 2021 FCA 88, paras. 4–8; National R&D Inc., 2020 TCC 47; Flavor Net, 2017 TCC 179; Income Tax Act, s. 248(1).

Although it worked in a systematic fashion, its work was characterized by the Crown's preferred expert as routine systems development (identifying requirements, prototyping with the CASE tool, testing, design refinement and iteration) directed at business requirements, commercial product evaluation, hardware configuration testing and routine software testing, rather than at formulating, testing and modifying hypotheses.

Must demonstrate adherence to the five-stage process: (a) observation of the problem; (b) clear objective; (c) articulation of technological uncertainty; (d) hypothesis formulation; and (e) methodical testing and modification of hypotheses based on trained observation and measurement. Blind "trial and error" or ad hoc parameter tweaking is legally insufficient. The Court evaluates the project globally over the taxation year (Les Abeilles, para. 153) for a logical progression between tests.
4. Technological Advancement (Generation of new scientific or technological knowledge advancing the baseline state of technology)
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, para. 17 (Criterion 4); Zeuter Development, 2006 TCC 597, para. 24; Hypercube Inc., 2015 TCC 65; Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c).

Argued that developing a very large, complex object-oriented system with a CASE tool and rapid prototyping constituted technological advancement. The courts accepted the Crown's expert evidence that, absent uncertainty not resolvable by standard practices, there was no technological advancement, and the IDLS was not shown to be more than a heavily customized variation on existing products.

The taxpayer must prove the process generated information that advances the understanding of scientific relations or technologies (even if the advance is slight or incremental, or consists of systematically rejecting a hitherto untested hypothesis). Creating a new commercial product, custom software, or novel feature configuration without advancing the underlying technological knowledge base does not qualify.
5. Progressive, Contemporaneous Documentation (Detailed record of hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed)
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, para. 17 (Criterion 5); RIS-Christie, 99 DTC 5087; 116736 Canada Inc., [1998] A.C.I. No. 478; Les Abeilles, 2014 TCC 313; Logix Data Products, 2021 TCC.

Did not retain documentation (including a detailed project management plan) that might have assisted it in discharging its onus, and called no witness directly involved in the development. Relied on an expert who had to infer the problems faced and the steps taken from the results of the work and the CASE tool's electronic logs.

While written contemporaneous reports are not an absolute statutory condition precedent if unimpeachable oral testimony is adduced (Les Abeilles; 116736 Canada Inc.), the absence of progressive records places the taxpayer in a "very precarious position." Courts routinely dismiss claims supported only by post-hoc consultant summaries or test logs lacking hypotheses, observations, and dated results (Kam-Press; Logix Data).
6. Expenditure Substantiation, Supporting Work Nexus & Exclusions (Commensurate supporting work, accurate labour costing, and exclusion of commercial/funded work)
Income Tax Act, s. 37(1), s. 127(5), s. 127(9), s. 248(1)(d)–(k); Concept Danat Inc., 2019 TCC 32, paras. 5–6, 20; Les Abeilles, 2014 TCC 313, paras. 25–36.

Claimed the cost of all developers and consultants directly involved in the IDLS development on an all-or-nothing basis (the expenditure figures were agreed), without segregating any eligible components from routine systems development; the Crown's expert considered much of the testing excludable as quality control or routine testing (now s. 248(1)(f)).

Supporting activities (programming, design, testing) under s. 248(1)(d) must be proven "commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of" core SR&ED under s. 248(1)(a)–(c). Labour costs cannot be substantiated by arbitrary year-end percentage estimates (Concept Danat); they require contemporaneous time-tracking tied to specific experimental tasks and formal "experimental deviation" records.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their advisors can proactively structure R&D operations to overcome the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 and its jurisprudential progeny, the following two applied industry case studies provide comprehensive, step-by-step remedial blueprints.
Case Study 1: Enterprise Software & Distributed Systems Engineering (Overcoming the "Custom Software & Unverifiable Architecture Hypothesis" Pitfall)
Baseline Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

BorderClear Logistics Technologies Inc. ("BorderClear"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Mississauga, Ontario, develops enterprise customs brokerage, tariff classification, and multi-modal freight clearance software. During its current taxation year, BorderClear undertakes a major $1.8 million software engineering initiative to replace its legacy monolithic, procedurally coded customs clearance system with a cloud-native, object-oriented, event-driven microservice architecture capable of processing real-time cross-border manifest streams.

Under its initial internal approach, BorderClear's Chief Technology Officer drafts a preliminary Form T661 technical narrative stating that the project's objective is to build a scalable object-oriented customs platform, and defines the hypothesis as: "Adopting a decoupled, object-oriented microservice architecture with reusable domain components will increase developer productivity by 35%, reduce new customs rule deployment time from weeks to hours, and allow the platform to process 50,000 manifest records per second." Developers log their hours to a single general Jira epic titled "NextGen Architecture Rewrite," and no progressive experimental test logs are maintained outside standard Git commits.

If filed in this state, BorderClear's claim will face certain disallowance upon CRA review and Tax Court appeal under C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393. Migrating from procedural code to an object-oriented microservice architecture constitutes routine software engineering using established design patterns under both C.W. Agencies and Hypercube Inc., 2015 TCC 65. Furthermore, the stated hypothesis regarding developer productivity and deployment time is a business and management proposition closely resembling the hypothesis that Judge Bonner found too vague to be proved or disproved by scientific research in C.W. Agencies (2000 DTC 2372, para. 23). Reliance on standard Git commits without documented experimental progression fails Criterion 3 under National R&D Inc., 2020 TCC 47 and Criterion 5 under Kam-Press, 2021 FCA 88, while lumping all rewrite hours into a single cost pool fails to segregate eligible supporting programming under paragraph 248(1)(d) from routine commercial coding and quality assurance excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i).
Step 1: Project Governance and Statutory Boundary Segregation

BorderClear must immediately restructure its project governance to separate its commercial software rewrite (the "Business Project") from the specific computer science bottlenecks that cannot be resolved using standard architectural patterns (the "SR&ED Project"). Prior to commencing experimental coding, the Vice President of Engineering and Tax Counsel establish an internal governance charter requiring a formal "Technological Uncertainty Gate Review". Under this protocol, routine software modules—such as user authentication, UI/UX dashboards, standard CRUD database persistence, REST API wrappers, and commercial EDI message parsing—are classified as ineligible commercial development and excluded from the SR&ED claim boundary ab initio.

Through a documented literature and public-domain benchmark review evaluating Apache Kafka, Redis Cluster, and standard JVM garbage collection specifications, the engineering team isolates a specific system-level technological limitation that defines the narrow SR&ED project. Specifically, when ingesting concurrent, out-of-order multi-modal freight telemetry streams at rates exceeding 40,000 events per second, standard optimistic concurrency control (OCC) and distributed two-phase commit (2PC) protocols within an object-oriented state machine cause non-deterministic thread lock contention and JVM heap fragmentation, resulting in tail latencies (p99) exceeding 4,200 milliseconds and state corruption. Standard public-domain solutions, such as horizontal sharding or off-the-shelf in-memory data grids, cannot resolve this bottleneck without violating strict cross-border customs transactional atomicity requirements.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Verifiable Hypothesis Formulation

To satisfy Judge Bonner's definition of a hypothesis in C.W. Agencies (para. 23) and Criterion 2 of 2001 FCA 393 (para. 17), BorderClear replaces its business and productivity hypothesis with falsifiable, variable-driven technological hypotheses that can be proved or disproved objectively through empirical measurement. First, the engineering team documents specifically what is lacking in the computer science knowledge base to satisfy Criterion 1: "It is unknown whether deterministic transactional state consistency can be maintained across distributed, asynchronous object-oriented state nodes under high-skew key distributions (>40,000 events/sec) while constraining serialization latency below 50 ms and bounding off-heap memory allocation overhead below 12%, given the fundamental trade-off between distributed lock-free consensus overhead and object serialization garbage collection pauses."

Next, instead of claiming that object-oriented architecture improves developer productivity, the team formulates specific provisional concepts linking independent algorithmic variables to measurable system outputs. For its primary experimental iteration (Hypothesis 1.1), BorderClear hypothesizes that if the state-mutation engine replaces standard heap-allocated object graphs with a custom off-heap, flyweight byte-buffer memory layout coupled with a deterministic vector-clock conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) merge algorithm (the independent variable), then thread lock contention during concurrent manifest state mutations will be eliminated and state-commit latency will be reduced below 45 ms at 50,000 events per second without breaking ACID-equivalent state determinism (the quantifiable effect), because JVM garbage collection traversal of nested object references is the primary driver of tail-latency spikes. When initial testing demonstrates that pure state-based CRDT merges increase network payload serialization overhead by 310% under deep object hierarchies—thereby falsifying Hypothesis 1.1—the team formulates a modified proposition (Hypothesis 1.2): if a hybrid delta-state causal ring-buffer with bounded epoch watermarking is implemented, network serialization overhead will remain below 15% while maintaining commit latency under 50 ms.
Step 3: Contractual Terms, IP Ownership, and Subcontractor/Client Structuring

To prevent statutory disqualification or ITC reductions under subsections 37(1), 127(9), and 248(1) of the Act, BorderClear's legal counsel restructures both its customer contracts and its third-party software contractor agreements. Because BorderClear is developing the new customs platform while onboarding an anchor enterprise client, the Master Services Agreement (MSA) is drafted as a standard commercial Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) subscription agreement rather than a custom contract to perform R&D on behalf of the client. The MSA explicitly stipulates that BorderClear retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property, algorithms, and source code, that the client pays strictly for commercial service-level availability with no milestone payments contingent upon conducting specific research or experimental development, and that BorderClear bears the full financial and technical risk of development failure. This contractual structure prevents client revenues from being characterized by the CRA as a "contract payment" as defined in subsection 127(9), which would otherwise reduce BorderClear's qualified SR&ED expenditures for investment tax credit purposes under subsection 127(18).

Concurrently, where BorderClear engages specialized Canadian distributed-systems consultants, the Independent Contractor Agreement specifies that the contractor performs experimental analysis and supporting programming "on behalf of" BorderClear in Canada pursuant to subsection 37(1) and paragraph 248(1)(d). The contract vests all intellectual property and experimental data exclusively in BorderClear upon creation, requires the contractor to operate under the direct technical supervision and experimental protocols of BorderClear's SR&ED Lead, prohibits subcontracting work outside Canada, and mandates itemized invoices segregating eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) supporting programming hours from routine commercial coding.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking and Contemporaneous Labour Costing Architecture

To satisfy Criteria 3 and 5 of C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393, para. 17) and avoid the evidentiary collapse seen in National R&D Inc. (2020 TCC 47), Logix Data Products (2021 TCC), and Concept Danat (2019 TCC 32), BorderClear implements an automated, contemporaneous documentation and time-tracking pipeline. The company configures a dedicated Confluence and Jira "SR&ED Experimental Registry" linked directly to isolated Git experimental branches (such as exp/hypothesis-1.1-offheap-crdt). Every experimental iteration generates a date-stamped, immutable Experimental Protocol Record documenting the specific Hypothesis ID and independent parameter changed, the controlled test environment and workload profile (a synthetic replay of 10 million skewed customs events), the quantitative telemetry captured via Prometheus and Grafana exports (heap allocation rate, GC pause duration, p99 latency, and state divergence count), the analytical conclusion explaining mathematically why the hypothesis was confirmed or falsified, and the explicit link to the subsequent hypothesis modification, thereby establishing the "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests" required by National R&D, 2020 TCC 47.

Rather than estimating developer percentages at year-end, engineers log daily hours in Jira against specific experimental ticket codes mapped to either Core Experimental Development under paragraph 248(1)(c) or Directly Supporting Activities under paragraph 248(1)(d)—specifically, writing the experimental code branch, building the synthetic load-testing harness, and executing the telemetry analysis. Weekly timesheets are reviewed and countersigned by the VP of Engineering, creating a contemporaneous audit trail linking T4 payroll wages directly to dated experimental logs.
Case Study 2: Advanced Industrial Manufacturing & Automated Process Engineering (Overcoming the "Equipment Parameter Trial-and-Error & Commercial Production Overlap" Pitfall)
Baseline Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

AeroTherm Composites & Sub-Assemblies Ltd. ("AeroTherm"), a precision manufacturing corporation operating a plant in Drummondville, Quebec, manufactures structural polymer-metal sub-assemblies for commercial appliance and HVAC original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). To prevent the offshoring of a major OEM supply contract, AeroTherm invests $950,000 during its fiscal year to develop a high-speed, automated thermo-mechanical forming and laser-assisted polymer bonding line capable of reducing part cycle time from 14.5 seconds to 6.5 seconds while replacing virgin ABS resin with a 100% recycled polypropylene-glass-fibre composite.

Under its unstructured shop-floor practices, AeroTherm's engineers halt the commercial assembly line for several hours each week to test different combinations of laser power, air pressure, platen temperature, and mould cooling rates on the existing machinery, alongside testing three different mould groove geometries. At year-end, AeroTherm retains an external SR&ED consultant on a contingency fee basis. Because the shop floor kept no formal experimental notebooks, the consultant interviews the plant manager and writes a post-hoc T661 narrative claiming that the hypothesis was "to find the optimal machine settings and mould design to bond recycled polypropylene within a 6.5-second cycle time without part warping". The company president estimates that 15% of all plant operator and engineering salaries over the year were devoted to these trials.

If audited by the CRA or litigated before the Tax Court of Canada, this claim will be disallowed in full under C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 and its manufacturing progeny. Adjusting existing machine settings (air, laser speed, temperature, pressure) within the OEM equipment's normal operating range is routine engineering and parameter optimization, not technological uncertainty, as held in Concept Danat Inc., 2019 TCC 32 and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd., 2010 TCC 319. Similarly, "trying to find a recipe" or optimal machine setting by random or sequential trial and error without a scientific hypothesis fails Criteria 2 and 3 of C.W. Agencies (Flavor Net, 2017 TCC 179; Docket 2014-1594(IT)I, para. 22). Relying on after-the-fact consultant summaries without progressive records is fatal under Criterion 5 (Kam-Press Metal Products, 2019 TCC 246, para. 29, aff'd 2021 FCA 88), and claiming a flat 15% management estimate of shop-floor salaries without segregating commercial production runs (excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i)) is invalid as a matter of law (Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32, para. 20).
Step 1: Project Governance and Formal "Experimental Deviation" Protocols

Drawing directly from the successful judicial precedent in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313—which applied C.W. Agencies to allow an SR&ED claim for assembly-line process development in Quebec—AeroTherm institutes a rigorous shop-floor governance protocol that legally and operationally separates experimental development from routine engineering and commercial production. As validated by Justice Jorré in Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313 at paras. 26–31), AeroTherm establishes a formal Quality and Engineering Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) classifying any departure from normal commercial production into three distinct categories: a Type A Deviation for material substitution (an ineligible routine production adjustment); a Type B Deviation for standard engineering or tooling changes (ineligible routine engineering or parameter tuning within OEM equipment specifications); and a Type C Deviation for experimental development (eligible SR&ED systematic investigation outside known equipment and material physics envelopes).

Whenever a Type C Experimental Deviation is scheduled during daily operational meetings, commercial production on the line must formally stop, with the stoppage logged via the plant Manufacturing Execution System (MES). During this window, the experimental tooling and hardware modifications are installed, the controlled experimental run is executed, all experimental parts produced during the window are quarantined and scrapped so they are never sold commercially (preventing any commercial production taint under paragraph 248(1)(i)), and the line is restored to its exact baseline configuration before commercial production resumes.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Physical/Material Hypothesis Formulation

To overcome the rulings in Jentel Manufacturing (2010 TCC 319), Concept Danat (2019 TCC 32), and C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393), AeroTherm shifts its technical narrative from "finding optimal machine settings" to resolving fundamental thermo-mechanical and polymer-physics incompatibilities that occur beyond the normal operating envelope of existing equipment. First, the engineering team documents the baseline engineering runs showing why routine engineering and OEM specifications failed under Criterion 1: when operating the laser and thermo-mechanical press within the manufacturer's standard parameter ranges, the recycled polypropylene-glass-fibre composite exhibits heterogeneous crystallinity and anisotropic thermal conductivity. Consequently, increasing laser energy to achieve a 6.5-second bond cycle causes localized thermal degradation (polymer chain scission) at the glass-fibre interface while leaving the core unbonded. Establishing that the equipment must be physically modified and operated outside its standard design envelope removes the project from the "routine settings" trap of Concept Danat.

Second, to satisfy Criterion 2 of C.W. Agencies, AeroTherm formulates falsifiable thermo-mechanical hypotheses linking material and energy variables to measurable structural outcomes. Specifically, under Hypothesis 2.1, the team postulates that because recycled polypropylene exhibits a 40% wider melting endotherm than virgin ABS due to variable molecular weight distribution, if the continuous-wave laser energy delivery is modified via a custom pulsed-modulation optical beam-shaper delivering a bimodal spatial energy profile (high-intensity perimeter pre-heat at 1,200 W followed by a modulated core soak) coupled with dynamic ultrasonic horn clamping (the independent variables), interfacial shear strength will exceed 12 MPa within a 6.5-second cycle while keeping surface thermal degradation below 0.5% by weight (the quantifiable effect), because pulsed energy relaxation intervals allow conductive heat dissipation past the reflective glass-fibre boundary layer.
Step 3: Contractual Terms, OEM Client Approvals, and Materials Exclusion Management

AeroTherm restructures its commercial supply contract with its OEM appliance client to protect its SR&ED claim from funded-research exclusions and commercial production disqualifications. In its OEM Supply Agreement, AeroTherm contracts solely to deliver finished sub-assembly parts at a fixed commercial unit price, while explicitly retaining exclusive ownership of all custom manufacturing processes, laser modulation hardware modifications, and process intellectual property developed on its shop floor. Even though the OEM client requires prior technical notification before AeroTherm tests a modified sub-assembly geometry—analogous to the Mabe client approval requirement recognized as compatible with SR&ED in Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313 at para. 28)—the contract stipulates that the OEM provides no direct reimbursement or guaranteed cost recovery for AeroTherm's experimental process trials, ensuring no "contract payment" reduction arises under subsection 127(18) of the Act.

Furthermore, under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED is an eligible expenditure; materials are consumed only where they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED, while materials transformed into a product that still has value remain exposed to investment tax credit recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36) if that product is sold or converted to commercial use. AeroTherm's ERP system assigns a dedicated "Type C Experimental Scrap" inventory code to all resin pellets, glass-fibre compounds, and metal inserts consumed during Type C line stoppages, documenting their physical destruction during destructive tensile-load testing so they are never commingled with commercial cost of goods sold.
Step 4: Progressive Shop-Floor Data Logging and Labour Substantiation

To satisfy Criteria 3 and 5 of C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393, para. 17) and prepare an evidentiary record capable of withstanding both a CRA RTA audit and Tax Court cross-examination, AeroTherm mandates progressive shop-floor dossiers for every Type C line stoppage. Completed contemporaneously before, during, and immediately after each test run, each Type C Experimental Dossier binds together the pre-test sheet stating the exact hypothesis being tested and the hardware or optical modification installed, automated PLC data-logger exports capturing millisecond-level temperature, laser pulse frequency, clamping pressure, and cycle duration during the run, destructive Instron tensile-testing lab reports and microscopic cross-section measurements quantifying bond shear strength (MPa) and polymer degradation on the test batch, and post-test engineering analysis explaining how the empirical data validated or refuted the hypothesis and dictating the parameters for the next Type C deviation.

During a Type C Experimental Deviation, as recognized in Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313 at para. 36), operating an experimental line test requires at least as many shop-floor operators, technicians, and engineers as regular commercial production. To claim these direct labour and paragraph 248(1)(d) supporting testing wages without relying on invalid percentage estimates (Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32), all participating engineers, toolmakers, and line operators swipe their electronic plant badges into the specific "Type C Deviation Work Order" when commercial production halts and swipe out the moment the line is restored to commercial production.
5. Synthesis of Doctrinal Evolution and Strategic Advisory Recommendations
Comparative Synthesis of Post-C.W. Agencies Jurisprudence

To contextualize how the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal have enforced the five criteria of C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 across diverse technical domains, the following table summarizes key subsequent Canadian decisions applying the ruling.

headers: Primary C.W. Agencies Criterion at Issue
Outcome & Key Doctrinal Takeaway for Canadian Practitioners

cells: Zeuter Development Corp. v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597
Custom Software Development (IC 97-1)
Criteria 1 & 4 (Technological Uncertainty & Advancement)

Appeal Dismissed: Resolving functional or project uncertainties associated with building a new software product is not resolving technological uncertainty; creating a new product does not automatically constitute a technological advancement.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2010 TCC 319 (aff'd 2011 FCA)
Plastics Thermoforming & Injection Moulding
Criteria 1 & 3 (Routine Engineering vs. Systematic Investigation)

Appeal Dismissed: Testing different commercial plastics (ABS, HDPE, polypropylene) and mould groove iterations using known thermoforming and injection moulding processes—and using a standard heat sink—constituted routine engineering rather than SR&ED.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313
Automated Assembly Line Process Engineering
Criteria 1, 3 & 5 (Global Project Evaluation, Expert Independence & Documentation)

Appeal Allowed: Each project must be evaluated globally over the taxation year, not each test in isolation (para. 153). While contemporaneous reports are not a strict statutory requirement if credible testimony and structured "deviation" procedures exist, CRA RTAs testifying as experts must offer independent technical opinions rather than merely reciting CRA policy.
Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65 (2015 DTC 1089)
Web Crawler & Website Verification Software
Criterion 1 (Technological Uncertainty vs. Competent Programmer Standard)

Appeal Dismissed: Developing software to inspect and verify websites involved normal analyses carried out by competent programmers using current technology and standard software development techniques.
Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32
Laser Fabric Engraving, Embroidery & Printing
Criteria 1, 3 & Costing (Equipment Settings, Trial-and-Error & Salary Estimates)

Appeal Dismissed: Testing combinations of settings within a machine's normal operating range involves no technological uncertainty. Random settings adjustments are ineligible trial and error, and retrospective percentage estimates of employee hours (e.g., 10.2%) cannot substantiate SR&ED claims.
National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (aff'd 2022 FCA 72)
Multi-Tenant Software Architecture & In-Memory Arrays
Criteria 2 & 3 (Logical Progression of Hypothesis Testing)

Appeal Dismissed: Even where genuine technological uncertainty is proven under Criterion 1, the claim fails under Criteria 2 and 3 if the taxpayer cannot demonstrate methodical hypothesis testing and a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests".
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)
Structural Metal & Tempered Glass Fabrication
Criterion 3 & 5 (Binding Status of Scientific Method & Consultant Summaries)

Appeal Dismissed: Confirmed via Canada Trustco statutory analysis that the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies (including adherence to the "scientific method") are binding law under s. 248(1). At trial (2019 TCC 246), reliance on after-the-fact consultant summaries lacking contemporaneous records was held fatal.

body.text: Actionable Conclusions for Canadian Tax Counsel and Technical Advisors

The enduring lesson of C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 is that the Canadian SR&ED regime does not subsidize commercial innovation, custom software engineering, or industrial problem-solving in the abstract; rather, it subsidizes the generation of new scientific or technological knowledge through the rigorous discipline of the scientific method. To insulate claims from reassessment and prevail in litigation before the Tax Court of Canada, corporate taxpayers and their legal advisors must enforce four integrated compliance imperatives across all R&D operations.

First, technical narratives on Form T661 must eliminate business and productivity objectives from hypothesis statements, never framing hypotheses around labour efficiency, developer productivity, cost reduction, or schedule compression. Every hypothesis must be drafted to satisfy Judge Bonner's description of a hypothesis as a provisional concept that may be proved or disproved objectively (2000 DTC 2372, para. 23) by stating a provisional causal relationship between a specific, manipulated technical parameter and a quantifiable technological metric that can be empirically observed, measured, and objectively proved or disproved. Second, because technological uncertainty under Criterion 1 of C.W. Agencies cannot exist where problems are solvable via routine engineering or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals, taxpayers must document the exhaustion of public-domain knowledge prior to claiming SR&ED, demonstrating specifically why standard architectures, commercial software libraries, or OEM equipment operating envelopes failed or were theoretically insufficient before experimental work began.

Third, while oral testimony is legally admissible in the Tax Court of Canada (Les Abeilles, 2014 TCC 313), relying on uncorroborated memory or post-hoc narratives drafted by external consultants invites almost certain dismissal under Criterion 5 of C.W. Agencies (Kam-Press, 2021 FCA 88; Logix Data Products, 2021 TCC). Engineering teams must therefore capture dated test logs showing the exact hypothesis tested, the quantitative measurements recorded, the analytical conclusion drawn, and how that conclusion dictated the modification of the hypothesis for the subsequent test (National R&D, 2020 TCC 47). Finally, taxpayers must replace year-end percentage salary estimates (Concept Danat, 2019 TCC 32) with contemporaneous work-order time tracking that strictly segregates core experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) and commensurate supporting work under paragraph 248(1)(d) from routine testing under paragraph 248(1)(f) and commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i), reinforced by formal shop-floor "experimental deviation" protocols (Les Abeilles, 2014 TCC 313) and IP-protective commercial contracts.

outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; FCA formally adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as binding appellate law.
